"A Cute Auto-Battler Undone by Monotony." Facehand initially captivates with its charming and cute aesthetics, offering an auto-battler roguelike experience that seems promising. The vibrant graphics and whimsical character designs create a delightful first impression. However, the charm quickly wears off as the game's flaws become apparent. The core issue lies in the gameplay loop, which becomes stale and repetitive after just a few hours. Despite the initial appeal, there’s a noticeable lack of depth and variety in the mechanics. The game doesn't introduce enough new content or challenges to keep it interesting over the long term. Each run starts to feel like a chore rather than a thrilling adventure, and the sense of progression is minimal. One of the most significant drawbacks is the RNG, which feels poorly balanced. Instead of adding an element of unpredictability and excitement, the randomness often leads to frustration. This makes it hard to strategize effectively and results in repetitive and unsatisfying gameplay sessions. You end up repeating the same battles, hoping for the right drops to progress, which quickly becomes monotonous. Overall, while Facehand has a solid foundation with its charming presentation and a few interesting ideas, it falls short in execution. The repetitive gameplay, frustrating RNG, and poorly designed achievements make it difficult to recommend. It’s a game that had potential but ultimately doesn’t deliver a satisfying experience. If you’re looking for a roguelike with lasting appeal and meaningful progression, you might want to look elsewhere.

非常好游戏，使我emoji旋转 看谜之声的视频知道了这个游戏，然后下了demo版一共爽玩23小时，很tm上头 正式版发售后下开的第一把就见到了一半以上的没见过的新牌，内容量相当丰富。我还是打了demo版里比较熟悉的敬礼女巫召唤流玩法，对于这个打法而言好像变化不大w 与demo版相比，正式版增加了很多新牌，肉眼可见的可以构建出更多样的玩法牌组（但我还是喜欢召唤流w） 卡牌的升级也优化了许多，不再锁上限3级，而是每3经验就能升1级。还有许多临时增加等级的卡牌（比如老师），导致更容易打出超高伤害（比如我打的第一局在25回合就打出了科学计数法，一把4.67e10的伤害） 此外打完一局25回合后还能开启无尽模式，可以测试自己的卡组最多能爆出多少伤害。当然玩到这个阶段的卡组应该都是有指数增长的能力的吧。 许多牌需要解锁，是一种提高游戏时长的方式，可以理解 每日挑战，这个挺有趣的。不过目前玩家不多，24/06/22的每日我打完显示共有19人通过，我是排行第7名 --2024/06/22 ===2025.5.16增加=== 感觉玩法不是很多，我玩了很多把还是只会玩敬礼女巫僵尸套装...

[h1][b]emoji也能自走棋[/b][/h1] [h1]前言[/h1] 《Facehand》是一款非常有意思的自走棋游戏，每局玩家都将控制5个单位对战敌人，不同的是本作中出现的所有角色及卡牌都是常见的emoji表情。 这些被广泛用于聊天的表情在本作中一跃成为主角，其中人物、动物等生物emoji是用来作战的单位，食物、物品、地点等emoji则成为了本作的遗物道具以及消耗品。 [h1]emoji大作战[/h1] 当前版本中，每轮游戏由25场战斗构成，每完成一场玩家都会获得金币奖励，其可用于购买上述内容。 其中作战emoji可以被强化和升级，强化是指提升其血量、攻击力等属性。 升级则是自走棋类游戏不可或缺的一环，不同的是本作中emoji不会自动升级，需要玩家手动拖拽相同的emoji来进行合成，而且这个合成也不限制相同等级，更方便构筑成型。 [h1]不错的自走棋体验[/h1] 每场战斗我们都将对战一个敌人，我方则需要派出5名emoji来对抗，这部分内容类似于《杀戮尖塔》，每回合系统都会从抽牌堆随机抽出一些emoji来供玩家调配。 作战的策略在于emoji的出战顺序，靠近敌人的emoji会率先出手，并且触发其被动效果，诸如为其他emoji增加生命值、攻击力、分裂开来等等，因此越强力的老大哥越要放到后排压轴。 之后就是自动战斗阶段了，如果觉得慢，还可以调整其对战速度，最近的版本中更是更新了跳过战斗环节直接显示结果的功能。 每场战斗拥有3次作战机会，花费更少的次数完成战斗能获得更多奖励，反之则宣告游戏失败。 [h1]结语[/h1] 《Facehand》整体设计的非常不错，可爱的emoji表情、清新的风格与快节奏的对战能让玩家快速上手，而自走棋关键的策略性也有着不错的体现。 另外本作整体特效与交互也做的非常棒，有种《小丑牌》的美，目前唯一的不足便是缺少中文支持，希望官方能尽快加入简体中文，让更多的玩家体验到这部作品。 [quote]欢迎关注我们的鉴赏家:[url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/35402982/]走心评测[/url] ←遵从内心，写出真实感受 欢迎加入我们Steam组:[url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/ZXPC]走心评测[/url]←点击加入，一起探索游戏的乐趣 喜欢这篇评论，也麻烦点个赞，让更多人能够看到！[/quote]

The fans of the emoji franchise have been abandoned for a long time, since the Emoji Movie, and we all know that was a dumpster fire hotter than the 🔥 emoji itself. Finally, the franchise has managed to break into the niche roguelike genre, and for the most part succeeded. At last, the emoji fanbase can have a good product on their hands - or should I say, on their Facehands? 🤚👀 This game is truly a 💎 in the rough. One major downside is the 🍆 emoji not being included. It would have been a perfect combo with the 🥵 emoji or 💪. Think of the missed opportunities! We could have had the ultimate 'gym bro' deck. 💪💦🍆 The absence of this crucial emoji is truly a tragedy of Shakespearean proportions. 😭 Overall, I'll have to give it 4/5 due to this critical fault. It's like ordering a pizza without cheese - still good, but missing that essential ingredient that would make it perfect. I'm excited to see more emoji-themed products, and I hope the franchise's fanbase continues to grow. Who knows? Maybe next time we'll get an emoji-based FPS where we can 360 no-scope with the 🎯 emoji.

Fun for the first couple hours when the game tricks you into believing there's a ton of viable builds, only to play a dozen more hours and find out that you will just be chasing the same overpowered combos all throughout your achievement grind, or waste entire runs trying to do something creative that just gets shuffled around by an anti-synergy boss mechanic and see an hour of your time wasted. I've seen enough. You might think I've had my money's worth of playtime, but games like these don't respect your time, they have a couple hours of good content at best, and then pretend there's an ocean of depth hidden behind 20 difficulty modifiers. There's not, it's mind numbingly boring and even if the couple powerful combos in the game were fun, padding them with trash bait makes for a stale game that left me feeling cheated. You want a real red flag that this game is stale boring trash that doesn't inspire any creative builds? Go check out the guides section. Notice how there's no posts about cool original builds, the only guide is for how to abuse a combo that breaks the game lmfao. Final verdict? If you've played all the other actual good games in this genre (Monster Train, Balatro, to name just two), then sure, get this one on sale. If you have S tier games in this genre to play still, wtf are you doing looking at this ugly emoji puke?

I don't like giving this a thumb down. This is a fun ass game. Simple concept, solid execution for the most part. Highly addictive and quite fun! So why no? Dev appears to be pump and dump type. Churning out small cheap games that are mashups/clones of other, more popular titles. Nothing really wrong with that, but this hasn't seen an update in 6 months at the time of writing. It could use a few more passes at balance, and optimization. It could also use some more content, paid or free. If the dev picks this back up (It's Jan '25 currently), then click the buy button. Otherwise go in informed. It's only $7 sure, but the game could also be so much more. This isn't a genre you can/should pump and dump in. It's really frustrating to see it done with such an excellent mash-up concept too.

Dev made a promising SAP clone that hundreds of people were playing, but they haven't updated it since the week they released it. They've since released another game and announced two different games.

Update (9.6 hours played): I previously *did* recommend this game, but have changed my mind. It's *fun*, but it has an utter lack of depth. There's basically one-right-way to play, so every run feels samey once you figure that out. There are 3 or 4 different strong decks you can build, which provides some replayability. Also there are "Grades" (increasing difficulties) that provide a little replayability butt MEH, they don't really spice things up at all. And the dev has never put out a content update as far as I can tell. I've won 3 runs, had my fun, and am probably done. For $8, it's not really a bad deal. But there's better games for the money. For contrast, Roll is a $5 game, I've played it over 100 hours, and it has had several content updates in the last 3 years. Shotgun King is a $10 game I've played for 70 hours. DigDigDrill was $4, and I only played a little over ten hours ... but it felt more rewarding than this game. More depth, more complexity, less bland. (4 hours played) I've only won one run, but I'm a big fan so far. I don't think its going to have massive replayability like Slay The Spire did, but we'll see how much the Grades and daily runs spice things up. Having alternate characters or formats or something woulda been cool. But game was $8 so as long as I get about 10 hours out of it, I'm happy, and I think I will. Edit (8 hours played): I've now tried out two distinctly different strategies, and super optimized one of them. There's at least one other main strategy to figure out. There's not much in-game incentive to play different strategies, unless Grades encourage this at higher levels, and the Dailies likely encourage certain strats. So choosing different strats seems to be a mostly self-directed activity. According to SteamDB, game does not go on sale often, and lowest price was $4.89. I don't think its worth waiting for a sale.

Facehand continues to surprise me with how enjoyable it is. I bought this, assuming it would be maybe 2 hours worth of enjoyment. And at first, that's what I got. I played a few runs, won one or two, and then put it down. But then after a while, it would pull me back in, and has done so a few times now. Despite it's simplicity, it is deceptively fun. My one gripe with the game is that I feel like there should just be one more additional strategy available. I say that, despite not having used every card yet, but it really does feel like there's one playstyle missing to feel completely there. Which is not to say that Facehand isn't a complete game, it definitely is. It just feels like, if there was one extra playstyle, the game would benefit so much more. But perhaps that would mess with the balance of the game, it's tough to tell. Either way, while Facehand is by no means treading new ground, it pulls off its shtick more than well enough to be a worthy addition to the library of those who like roguelike deckbuilders and/or autobattlers. PS: Unfortunately does not work on Steam Deck. While most actions are theoretically doable with the touchscreen, or the mousepad, the act of removing a card does not seem possible, since the game always assumed I wanted to actively drag a card if I ever touched it. A shame, and I'd love to see an update that made it work properly.

Facehand is a roguelike autobattler that takes a deceptively simple concept and turns it into an extremely addictive strategy experience built around chaining absurd combinations together. Developed and published by foolsroom, the game mixes elements of deckbuilding, auto-combat strategy, and synergy management into a fast-paced loop where players assemble teams of strange emoji-like units capable of producing increasingly chaotic interactions. At first glance, the colorful presentation and goofy visual style may make the game appear lightweight or casual, but beneath that simplicity is a surprisingly deep system centered entirely around experimentation, optimization, and discovering game-breaking combinations. The gameplay revolves around constructing powerful “hands” made up of units, relics, runes, and passive effects that automatically activate during combat. Battles play out on their own once preparations are complete, meaning the real challenge lies in strategic planning rather than direct action. Players must carefully decide which units to purchase, where to place them, and how to build around certain synergies that can scale dramatically over the course of a run. This structure creates a constant sense of experimentation because nearly every successful run emerges from discovering combinations that unexpectedly spiral into massive chains of destruction. One of the game’s greatest strengths is how rewarding its combo systems feel. Certain units and relics interact in ways that create explosive chain reactions capable of completely overwhelming enemy encounters. Some builds revolve around rapid attack loops, while others focus on status effects, scaling damage, heat generation, or bizarre support interactions that multiply power exponentially. Watching a carefully assembled setup activate perfectly during battle is incredibly satisfying because victories feel earned through planning and creativity rather than raw luck alone. The game constantly encourages players to push its systems to the limit in search of the next overpowered strategy. What makes Facehand especially addictive is the pace of progression. Runs move quickly, unlocks arrive regularly, and new relics or unit combinations consistently introduce fresh possibilities. The game avoids becoming overly complicated during the early hours, gradually introducing mechanics in a way that feels approachable even for players unfamiliar with autobattlers or roguelike deckbuilders. At the same time, the strategic depth increases significantly once players begin understanding how different systems interact. Small adjustments in positioning or relic selection can dramatically affect the outcome of an entire run, giving the game a surprisingly high skill ceiling despite its simple appearance. The progression system also does a good job of rewarding repeated play. Unlockable content steadily expands the pool of available strategies, encouraging experimentation with different archetypes and combinations. Some runs naturally evolve into defensive setups focused on survival, while others become aggressive engines of nonstop attacks and infinite scaling effects. The game thrives on these moments of discovery, where a seemingly weak build suddenly transforms into something unstoppable due to one perfectly timed relic or synergy. Visually, Facehand embraces an intentionally silly and minimalist aesthetic built around expressive emoji-inspired designs and colorful visual effects. While the art style will not appeal to everyone, it gives the game a distinct personality that separates it from more serious-looking strategy titles. The simplicity of the visuals also works in the game’s favor because it keeps the increasingly chaotic battles readable even when dozens of abilities are triggering simultaneously. Effects are flashy enough to make powerful combinations feel impactful without completely overwhelming the screen. The soundtrack and sound effects are relatively understated but effective enough to support the gameplay loop. Most of the excitement comes from watching strategies unfold during battles, and the game wisely keeps the audio from becoming distracting during long sessions. Short runs and fast pacing also help maintain momentum, making it easy to jump into “just one more run” repeatedly without noticing how much time has passed. However, Facehand does have several issues that become more noticeable over extended play sessions. Balance is probably the biggest problem. Some builds and synergies are dramatically stronger than others, which can eventually reduce strategic variety once players discover the most efficient combinations. While uncovering broken strategies is undeniably fun at first, certain setups become so dominant that experimenting with weaker archetypes can feel unnecessary. This imbalance occasionally makes the game feel easier than intended once players fully understand the systems. Replayability is strong initially, but repetition can eventually set in due to the relatively limited amount of content compared to larger roguelike deckbuilders. Enemy encounters and strategic patterns begin feeling familiar after many runs, especially once players settle into preferred strategies. Some later stages can also feel more automatic than strategic when overpowered builds are assembled early enough. The game remains entertaining because of its satisfying combo systems, but players looking for endless long-term variety may eventually want more content and mechanics. Another criticism involves the game’s long-term support. Community discussions frequently mention concerns about the pace of updates and the lack of significant post-launch expansion. The current version already provides a solid and highly enjoyable experience, but there is a lingering sense that the game’s systems could grow into something even larger with more content, balance adjustments, and additional gameplay modes. The foundation is excellent, which makes the absence of more aggressive post-launch support slightly disappointing for players hoping the game would continue evolving. Despite these flaws, Facehand succeeds because its core gameplay loop is incredibly satisfying. The combination of autobattling, roguelike progression, and absurd synergy experimentation creates a formula that is difficult to stop playing once the systems begin revealing their depth. Every run offers opportunities to discover new combinations, exploit powerful interactions, and push builds toward ridiculous levels of efficiency. The game also benefits from understanding exactly what makes strategy-focused roguelikes enjoyable. It does not overload players with unnecessary complexity or excessive management systems. Instead, it focuses almost entirely on delivering rewarding combinations and satisfying progression. This clarity of design helps the game remain accessible while still offering enough strategic depth to keep dedicated players engaged for dozens of hours. Facehand may not have the massive content pool or polish of genre giants, but it absolutely succeeds at creating an addictive and highly entertaining strategy experience built around experimentation and creativity. For players who enjoy roguelike deckbuilders, autobattlers, or synergy-heavy strategy games where discovering broken combinations is half the fun, Facehand offers a surprisingly deep and rewarding experience hidden beneath its goofy exterior. Rating: 8/10
